entries.entry: Katz, L. & Frost, R. (1992). The reading process is different for different orthographies: The orthographic depth hypothesis. In R. Frost & L. Katz (Eds.), *Orthography, Phonology, Morphology, and Meaning* (Advances in Psychology, Vol. 94, pp. 67–84). North-Holland/Elsevier. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0166-4115(08)62789-2; Frost, R., Katz, L. & Bentin, S. (1987). Strategies for visual word recognition and orthographical depth: A multilingual comparison. *Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance*, 13(1), 104–114. https://doi.org/10.1037/0096-1523.13.1.104; Frost, R. (1994). Toward a strong phonological theory of visual word recognition: True issues and false trails. In R. Frost & L. Katz (Eds.), *Orthography, Phonology, Morphology, and Meaning* (Advances in Psychology, Vol. 94, pp. 275–298). North-Holland/Elsevier.
entries.note: Canonical statements: (1) Katz & Frost (1992) chapter in Advances in Psychology Vol 94 (pp. 67–84) — the original ODH formulation; (2) Frost, Katz & Bentin (1987) JEP:HPP — empirical multilingual comparison; (3) Frost (1994) chapter in same volume (pp. 275–298) — within-item Hebrew pointed/unpointed comparison.

entries.entry: (a) Coltheart, M., Davelaar, E., Jonasson, J. T. & Besner, D. (1977). Access to the internal lexicon. In S. Dornic (Ed.), *Attention and Performance VI* (pp. 535–555). Lawrence Erlbaum Associates/Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003309734-29; (b) Frost, R. (1994). Toward a strong phonological theory of visual word recognition: True issues and false trails. In R. Frost & L. Katz (Eds.), *Orthography, Phonology, Morphology, and Meaning* (Advances in Psychology, Vol. 94, pp. 275–298). North-Holland/Elsevier; (c) Coltheart, M., Davelaar, E., Jonasson, J. T. & Besner, D. (1977) — the same chapter defines orthographic neighbourhood (N) as 'the set of words that can be formed by changing a single letter of the target word', the canonical statement for the neighbourhood/confusability effect used to justify nearest-neighbour decoy rules.
entries.note: All three verified. (a) Chapter in Attention and Performance VI (1977), pp. 535–555, defines orthographic neighbourhood N. (b) Frost (1994) in same Advances in Psychology Vol 94 as Katz & Frost (1992). (c) The Coltheart et al. (1977) chapter is the canonical source for orthographic neighbourhood definition and confusability effects.
